note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: Burning/stinging pain with urination; no identifiable food, drug, or environmental trigger. No concurrent ENT-related trigger reported.
- Symptom timeline and progression: Onset ~3 days ago; constant with each void; mild lower-abdominal “crampy” discomfort; one episode of visible blood in urine earlier today; malodorous urine noted. No progression to systemic or airway symptoms.
- ENT symptoms: Denies throat swelling/closure sensation, voice change, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, nasal/ocular symptoms, stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea, facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling at this time. Reports prior medication (clindamycin) allergy causing swelling (site and severity not specified).
- Relevant past episodes and treatments: No prior similar urinary episode reported. History of IBS. Tried OTC bicarbonate (unsuccessful). No prior epinephrine use or ED visits for allergy.
- Allergies and current medications:
  • Drug allergy: Clindamycin → swelling (details not documented).  
  • Current meds: None.  
  • New prescription planned: Nitrofurantoin or Trimethoprim 1 tab BID × 3 days (dose/strength not documented).
- Social context: 19-year-old college student; lives with friends; sexually active with new boyfriend (uses condoms); no smoking; social alcohol; able to seek help if needed.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: None reported/observed during tele-visit.
- Airway/breathing: No stridor, wheeze, or respiratory distress reported.
- Mental status: Alert, conversant.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded (tele-visit).
- Presence of another person with patient: Not applicable/unstated.

Assessment:
- Working clinical impression: Uncomplicated acute bacterial cystitis.
  Evidence: 3-day history of dysuria, suprapubic discomfort, malodorous urine, single episode macroscopic hematuria; absence of fever, flank pain, or systemic features.
- Differential diagnosis (from DDx, aligned with transcript):
  1. Uncomplicated acute cystitis – high likelihood; classic symptom cluster in young sexually active female.
  2. Chlamydial/gonococcal urethritis or cervicitis – medium likelihood; new partner, no prior STI screen; lacks discharge (opposing evidence).
  3. Urolithiasis – low-medium likelihood; hematuria supports, absence of flank/colicky pain opposes.
  (No ENT-specific conditions currently suspected.)
- No current evidence of ENT/allergic emergency; clindamycin allergy noted for future prescribing.

Plan:
- Pharmacologic: Start empiric antibiotic (Nitrofurantoin or Trimethoprim) 1 tablet twice daily for 3 days; pharmacy to supply appropriate formulation per guidelines considering local resistance patterns and clindamycin allergy.
- Supportive care: Increase oral fluids; consider cranberry products for symptomatic relief.
- Activity/sexual health: Advise abstaining from sexual intercourse until symptoms resolve; continue condom use thereafter; recommend first-time STI screening at local clinic.
- Monitoring & escalation (“red flags”): Seek immediate care for fever, flank/back pain, worsening abdominal pain, persistent hematuria, vomiting, or any new ENT/allergic symptoms (throat tightness, lip/tongue swelling, breathing difficulty).
- Follow-up: If no improvement by end of week or if red flags develop, contact clinic for reassessment; urine culture or further evaluation may be required. Consider ENT/allergy referral only if future drug-related swelling affects airway.
- Education: Reviewed proper antibiotic use, hydration, and avoidance of known allergen (clindamycin). Explained likelihood of simple UTI and low risk of serious complications with prompt treatment.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing but expected: Vital signs, focused abdominal/ENT exam findings, urinalysis or urine culture results, detail regarding severity/site of previous clindamycin-induced swelling, documentation of antibiotic choice/dosage/strength.  
● Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; minor conversational overlap but adequate clinical detail.
